"title": "Stable open-shell aromatic nitric acid radicals: accessing highly efficient photothermal conversion with restricted radiative decay",
"authors": "Zejun Wang, Jiawen Zhou, Yiheng Zhang, Weiya Zhu, Yuan Li",
"field_subfield": "Organic photothermal materials / radical chemistry / solar-driven water evaporation",
"type_of_paper": "Research article (materials synthesis and characterization)",
"executive_summary": "Open-shell organic radicals are usually unstable in air because of unsatisfied valency, which has limited their use as photothermal materials. This work introduces aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs), a class of neutral conjugated nitrogen-oxide radicals that lack steric hindrance protecting groups yet remain thermodynamically and kinetically stable in air. The authors prepared a series of star-shaped ANARs by demethylating phenolic hydroxyl precursors followed by air oxidation, yielding four compounds: TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8. Characterization by cyclic voltammetry, UV-vis-NIR spectroscopy, photoluminescence quantum yield measurements, electron spin resonance, and IR thermography established that these radicals are electrochemically reversible, highly air-stable, and possess high spin concentration. The central finding is that high spin concentration drives strongly enhanced nonradiative decay and suppressed radiative decay, which translates into excellent photothermal conversion. The best performer, TPA-TPA-O6, shows broadband absorption extending to 2000 nm, rapid temperature rise under an 808 nm laser, and outstanding stability over ten on/off cycles. In an interfacial solar evaporation system based on polyurethane foam loaded with TPA-TPA-O6, the material achieved a solar-to-vapor efficiency of 89.41% and a water evaporation rate of 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ under 1 sun, among the top values for pure organic small-molecule photothermal materials. The material also demonstrated negligible photobleaching and effective seawater desalination. The study positions stable high-spin radicals as a promising, low-cost, and reproducible strategy for solar energy conversion and identifies future directions in organic electronics, spintronics, and magnetic devices.",

summary.title: Stable open-shell aromatic nitric acid radicals: accessing highly efficient photothermal conversion with restricted radiative decay
summary.authors: Zejun Wang, Jiawen Zhou, Yiheng Zhang, Weiya Zhu, Yuan Li
summary.field_subfield: Organic photothermal materials / radical chemistry / solar-driven water evaporation
summary.executive_summary: Open-shell organic radicals are usually unstable in air because of unsatisfied valency, which has limited their use as photothermal materials. This work introduces aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs), a class of neutral conjugated nitrogen-oxide radicals that lack steric hindrance protecting groups yet remain thermodynamically and kinetically stable in air. The authors prepared a series of star-shaped ANARs by demethylating phenolic hydroxyl precursors followed by air oxidation, yielding four compounds: TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8. Characterization by cyclic voltammetry, UV-vis-NIR spectroscopy, photoluminescence quantum yield measurements, electron spin resonance, and IR thermography established that these radicals are electrochemically reversible, highly air-stable, and possess high spin concentration. The central finding is that high spin concentration drives strongly enhanced nonradiative decay and suppressed radiative decay, which translates into excellent photothermal conversion. The best performer, TPA-TPA-O6, shows broadband absorption extending to 2000 nm, rapid temperature rise under an 808 nm laser, and outstanding stability over ten on/off cycles. In an interfacial solar evaporation system based on polyurethane foam loaded with TPA-TPA-O6, the material achieved a solar-to-vapor efficiency of 89.41% and a water evaporation rate of 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ under 1 sun, among the top values for pure organic small-molecule photothermal materials. The material also demonstrated negligible photobleaching and effective seawater desalination. The study positions stable high-spin radicals as a promising, low-cost, and reproducible strategy for solar energy conversion and identifies future directions in organic electronics, spintronics, and magnetic devices.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
Open-shell organic radicals are usually unstable in air because of unsatisfied valency, which has limited their use as photothermal materials. This work introduces aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs), a class of neutral conjugated nitrogen-oxide radicals that lack steric hindrance protecting groups yet remain thermodynamically and kinetically stable in air. The authors prepared a series of star-shaped ANARs by demethylating phenolic hydroxyl precursors followed by air oxidation, yielding four compounds: TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8. Characterization by cyclic voltammetry, UV-vis-NIR spectroscopy, photoluminescence quantum yield measurements, electron spin resonance, and IR thermography established that these radicals are electrochemically reversible, highly air-stable, and possess high spin concentration. The central finding is that high spin concentration drives strongly enhanced nonradiative decay and suppressed radiative decay, which translates into excellent photothermal conversion. The best performer, TPA-TPA-O6, shows broadband absorption extending to 2000 nm, rapid temperature rise under an 808 nm laser, and outstanding stability over ten on/off cycles. In an interfacial solar evaporation system based on polyurethane foam loaded with TPA-TPA-O6, the material achieved a solar-to-vapor efficiency of 89.41% and a water evaporation rate of 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ under 1 sun, among the top values for pure organic small-molecule photothermal materials. The material also demonstrated negligible photobleaching and effective seawater desalination. The study positions stable high-spin radicals as a promising, low-cost, and reproducible strategy for solar energy conversion and identifies future directions in organic electronics, spintronics, and magnetic devices.

Research Context
Open-shell radicals are usually unstable in air due to unsatisfied valency. Radicals have potential applications across many functional fields. Organic small molecules are underexplored relative to inorganic and polymeric photothermal materials. Inorganic photothermal materials raise health and environmental concerns. Conjugated polymers suffer from reproducibility and stability problems. Stable neutral radicals are rarely reported and are hard to prepare. Photothermal materials convert NIR light into heat via nonradiative decay.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can air-stable open-shell radicals serve as efficient photothermal materials? Do steric hindrance groups protect radicals, or can unprotected radicals be stable? Does high spin concentration enhance nonradiative decay and photothermal conversion? Will TPA-TPA-O6 outperform other ANARs in photothermal and evaporation performance? Can these radicals achieve top-tier solar evaporation among pure organic materials?

Methodological Details
Four star-shaped ANAR materials were synthesized. Materials were made by demethylation and air oxidation of phenolic precursors. Different cores were introduced to vary electronic properties. Precursors were methoxy-substituted phenols. Cyclic voltammetry used specific electrolyte and conditions. Radicals were coated on carbon-glass electrodes to form films. Potentials were referenced to SCE with ferrocene internal standard. HOMO and LUMO levels were derived from CV curves. ESR used a fixed sample amount to compare spin concentration. PLQY was measured in solution and film. Photothermal tests used an 808 nm laser at 0.8 W cm⁻². Temperature was monitored with an IR thermal camera. Evaporation used PU foam loaded by impregnation and drying. The evaporation foam had a 2.0 cm diameter with 30 mg loading. Seawater desalination tested four primary ions. Detailed synthetic schemes are in the supporting information.

Procedures And Architectures
Synthesis proceeded in two main steps from precursors. Radicals were generated by oxidation of phenolic hydroxyl groups. CV curves were recorded over 15 cycles for stability. HOMO levels were measured at approximately -4.90 eV for TPA-TPA-O6. Demethylation quenched fluorescence to below 1% PLQY. High spin concentration was confirmed by ESR signal increase. Strong donor-acceptor conjugation reduced bandgap and enhanced paramagnetism. TPA-TPA-O6 showed broadband absorption extending to 2000 nm. Photothermal conversion was measured under 808 nm laser irradiation. TPA-TPA-O6 reached ~250 °C at higher laser power. Stability was verified over ten laser on/off cycles. PU foam was loaded by impregnation and drying at 80 °C. Equilibrium temperature reached 81.2 °C under continuous irradiation. Evaporation efficiency was calculated from mass change curves. Desalination reduced all four primary seawater ions.

Key Results
TPA-TPA-O6 film showed a large red shift versus its precursor. TPA-TPA-O6 exhibited a long radical absorption tail to 825 nm. TPA-TPA-O6 powder appeared black due to wide visible absorption. TPA-PY-O8 and TPA-TPZ-O6 showed absorption edges near 1000 nm and 800 nm. All radicals were electrochemically reversible over 15 cycles. TPA-TPA-O6 HOMO was -4.90 eV. TPA-TPA-O6 HOMO was enhanced versus its methoxy precursor. All radicals showed PLQY below 1%. TPA-TPA-O6 PLQY was 0.1%. TPA-TPZ-O6 PLQY was 0.9%. TPA-PY-O8 PLQY was 1.0%. Spiro-O8 PLQY was 0.3%. ESR signal increased markedly after demethylation. TPA-TPA-O6 and Spiro-O8 showed enhanced ESR signal intensity. High spin concentration led to nonradiative decay and photothermal enhancement. TPA-TPA-O6 temperature rose to ~210 °C in 60 s. TPA-TPA-O6 was stable over ten laser cycles. TPA-TPA-O6 evaporation rate was 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹. TPA-TPA-O6 evaporation efficiency was 89.41%. TPA-TPA-O6 foam equilibrium temperature reached 81.2 °C. TPA-TPA-O6 foam was ~10 °C hotter than bare PU foam. Desalination reduced all four primary ions below membrane methods.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Rich resonance structures confer stability to ANARs. High spin concentration drives nonradiative decay. Restricted radiative decay favors photothermal conversion. Donor-acceptor conjugation tunes bandgap and paramagnetism. TPA-TPA-O6 combines wide absorption with high paramagnetism. The design enables low-cost, reproducible organic photothermal materials. The strategy opens new directions for radical-based functional materials. Future work targets organic electronics, spintronics, and magnetic devices.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper relies heavily on supporting information for details. Exact PLQY values are only in the supporting information. HOMO/LUMO values are tabulated rather than stated in text. Some spectral descriptions appear garbled or OCR-corrupted. Exact evaporation efficiency calculation is in the supporting information. Comparison with reported materials relies on literature values. The study is limited to four ANAR compounds.

Claims
Aromatic nitric acid radicals are air-stable open-shell radicals suitable for photothermal conversion. ANARs are stable without protecting groups. ANARs show high thermal and electrochemical stability. ANARs are reversible over 15 CV cycles. Open-shell radicals are generally unstable in air. Some ANARs show poor photothermal performance. Stable radicals enable multifunctional applications. The strategy supports future electronic and spintronic devices.
High spin concentration enhances nonradiative decay and photothermal conversion efficiency. High spin concentration leads to nonradiative decay. TPA-TPA-O6 has high spin concentration. TPA-TPA-O6 temperature rose rapidly. TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 have low spin concentration. TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 rise only to ~40 °C. Restricted radiative decay favors photothermal materials. Donor-acceptor design can tune radical photothermal behavior.
TPA-TPA-O6 achieves top-tier solar-driven water evaporation among pure organic materials. TPA-TPA-O6 evaporation rate was 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹. TPA-TPA-O6 evaporation efficiency was 89.41%. TPA-TPA-O6 represents top performance in pure organic materials. The efficiency calculation is in the supporting information. Comparison relies on literature-reported values. The material enables effective seawater desalination. The material shows negligible photobleaching.

Data And Code Availability
Supporting information is available free of charge.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
TPA-TPA-O6 was stable over ten laser cycles. TPA-TPA-O6 temperature scaled with laser power. TPA-TPA-O6 temperature returned to ambient after laser off. TPA-TPA-O6 foam outperformed bare PU foam. TPA-TPA-O6 showed negligible photobleaching. TPA-TPA-O6 reduced all four primary seawater ions.

Ethical Considerations
The material avoids heavy metal ion poisoning. The material is biocompatible for biological applications. The material uses green solvents for processing. The material is low-cost and sustainable.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 2A shows UV-Vis absorption of TPA-TPA-OMe. Figure 2B and 2C show absorption of pyrene and triazine cores. Figure 3 shows reversible CV curves. Figure 4A shows ESR spectra. Figure 4B shows PLQY emission between 450 and 570 nm. Figure 4D links spin concentration to photothermal conversion. Figure 5A and 5C show temperature increments. Figure 6A shows photothermal conversion under 808 nm laser. Figure 6C shows stability over ten laser cycles. Figure 6E shows foam temperature under 1 sun. Figure 6F shows mass change curves for evaporation. Figure S17 and Table S2 compare reported materials.

Three Takeaways
The core contribution is a stable, low-cost, high-spin radical photothermal platform. The strongest evidence is the 89.41% efficiency and 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ rate. The future path is extending ANARs to electronics, spintronics, and magnetic devices.
